items.title: Former Porn Star Reveals Key to Unlocking Shame, Embracing Freedom
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Shame is not God's intention for your life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

If anyone knows the grip of shame, it’s a former porn star.

Joshua Broome spent years in the pornography industry before finding faith in God, abandoning a life driven by sexual sin and drug abuse, and becoming a husband and father to four boys.

Since his salvation 11 years ago, Broome has become an outspoken evangelist and advocate against the dangers of pornography. One of the barriers to healing, he explained to CBN News, is shame.

“Shame is not God’s intention for your life,” he said. “The solution to shame is connection, is confession.”

Before he learned the Gospel, Broome said it was shame — rather than enjoyment— that kept him trapped in the pornography industry for years. He explained that, while guilt reveals, “I’ve done something wrong,” shame wrongly convinces a person, “I am someone wrong.”

“If I believe that my only value is indicative of me selling myself for sex, well, then, of course I’m going to continue doing what I’ve done, because it’s just an overflow of who I am,” he said.

From the Old to the New Testament, the Bible is clear about the need for confession for spiritual healing.

In Proverbs 28:13, King Solomon wrote, “People who conceal their sins will not prosper, but if they confess and turn from them, they will receive mercy” (NLT).

Then, in 1 John 1:8-9, it’s written, “If we claim we have no sin, we are only fooling ourselves and not living in the truth. But if we confess our sins to him, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleans us from all wickedness” (NLT).

And in James 5:16, James wrote, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results” (NLT).

The key to breaking the cycle of shame, Broome emphasized, is honest and complete confession.

“The depth of your confession is going to equate to the level of your healing,” he said. “So say all of it.”

He continued, “The way that you own your past is you have to own it, and the way that you own it is you say it out loud because we can only be as free as we’re willing to be honest.”

For many, Broome said, the root of pornography use is not lust or even sex; more often than not, it’s tied to something much deeper: insecurity, loneliness, an unhealthy understanding of intimacy.

The truth is conversations about past sins or sin struggles are not easy. Broome and his wife, Hope, have had their fair share of difficult conversations over his sexual history. But the truth is, while accountability and responsibility are essential to spiritual growth, confession should be met with compassion.

“[My wife] looked at me and said, ‘Hey, I don’t want to minimize your pain … but I do want to tell you that you’re not defined by the worst thing you’ve ever done, and you won’t be defined by the greatest thing you ever do, because you’re not the author of you — God is,'” Broome recalled. “At the cross, the worst of us meets the best of God, and He wins. That’s how you defeat shame.”

Broome and his wife are the hosts of a new six-part series from XO Marriage, “Made Whole: Healing, Wholeness, and Holiness in a Sex-Saturated World.” You can access the course for free here.

Watch our wide-ranging conversation with Broome in the video above.

items.title: Celebrity Wishes for Perez Hilton’s Recovery — Then Takes It Back: Why?
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Perez Hilton’s livestream was the stuff of nightmares — a potentially demonic episode — and has laid bare the dark underbelly of social media, in more ways than one.

On the periphery of the scandal, a TikTok live video feed that ran nearly half an hour and showed Hilton covered in blood and repeatedly harming himself, was another troubling indication of cultural decay: a society that cares not about praying for our enemies but about getting even.

Jared Padalecki, who rose to fame in the early 2000s as one of the stars of “Gilmore Girls,” has used his clout to advocate for mental wellness, so it’s particularly striking to see him not only rescind but apologize for wishing Hilton well amidst his recovery from what was and will be a decisively defining and deeply dark moment in his life.

Initially, Padalecki wrote on social media, “I hope you are trying as best as you can to be kind to yourself right now. Please surround yourself with the love and support that all humans deserve.”

It wasn’t long before the “Supernatural” star faced swift condemnation for his kindhearted message to the celebrity gossip blogger. Padalecki deleted the post and apologized for publicly hoping for healing for Hilton, telling critics he “didn’t know” about the columnist’s career.

Padalecki went on to apologize for his “words caus[ing] any harm” and added he hopes everyone is “taking care of yourselves.”

It was Padalecki’s first instinct — his wish for Hilton’s healing — that was correct, regardless of Hilton’s checkered past and his indefensible work as a gossip blogger, actions that undoubtedly caused harm to the celebrities who were subject to his coverage.

That’s exactly what Jesus commands of us as His followers in Matthew 5:44-47 (NLT).

“But I say to you,” Jesus preached, “love your enemies! Pray for those who persecute you! In that way, you will be acting as true children of your Father in heaven.”

He went on to say, “For He gives His sunlight to both the evil and the good, and He sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. If you love only those who love you, what reward is there for that? Even corrupt tax collectors do that much. If you are kind only to your friends, how are you different from anyone else? Even pagans do that.”

Then, in Romans 12:17-21 (NLT), the Apostle Paul warned against taking revenge or seeking vengeance against others:

Never pay back evil with more evil. Do things in such a way that everyone can see you are honorable. Do all that you can to live in peace with everyone. Dear friends, never take revenge. Leave that to the righteous anger of God. For the Scriptures say, ‘I will take revenge; I will pay them back,’ says the Lord.

Instead, ‘If your enemies are hungry, feed them. If they are thirsty, give them something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals of shame on their heads.’

Don’t let evil conquer you, but conquer evil by doing good.

Our petition for God to intervene for the healing of another human being made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) should never be predicated on what he or she has done in the past. Rather, it should be evidence of an outpouring of gratitude for a forgiveness gifted to us by a Savior who asks each of us to forgive one another in the same way God, through Jesus, has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32).

Hilton, who in recent months has professed a faith in Jesus, needs prayer — regardless of the sins of his past.

All of us should absolutely be held accountable for our errors, missteps, and wrongdoings; taking responsibility for our actions is a necessary consequence of the choices we each make in this life. None of that, though, absolves us of the duty to pray for those around us or to need the prayers of others.

In the King James Version translation of 1 Peter 2:9, the Apostle Peter wrote that believers are “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people” in the world.

While social media is preying on our worst instincts — our fallen nature — to belittle, disparage, and denigrate, we follow a God who is calling us to do the opposite, to be peculiar by praying for the redemption of those trapped in dark places distant from the Lord.

As the psalmist wrote, I pray that, even as Hilton walks through the “darkest valley,” he would find the Shepherd who “leads me beside peaceful streams,” “renews my strength,” and “guides me along right paths” (Psalm 23:1-4, NLT).

items.title: Living Out God’s Love
items.author: Tim Gustafson
items.summary: Branden’s father was dying of cancer in his fifties. Wanting to help, Branden talked his parents into moving in with him so he could assist them. His dad loved the tropics but could no longer travel, so Branden got creative. He landscaped a pond behind his house, stocked it with fish, and inst
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Branden’s father was dying of cancer in his fifties. Wanting to help, Branden talked his parents into moving in with him so he could assist them. His dad loved the tropics but could no longer travel, so Branden got creative. He landscaped a pond behind his house, stocked it with fish, and installed a waterfall that tumbled over rocks. He trucked in three loads of beach sand, added banana trees, lights, and tiki torches, and built an awning for shade. His dad spent his last days enjoying a backyard island paradise.

Branden’s actions reflect the kind of harmony between parents and children envisioned in Exodus 20. There, God through Moses instructed the children of Israel: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12). That directive grows out of the commands to love and respect our heavenly Father (vv. 3-8) and bridges to the last five commands, which instruct us how to love and respect our fellow human beings. Don’t murder, don’t commit adultery, don’t steal, don’t lie, don’t covet (vv. 12-17).

Honoring parents might come easily for some. For others, it’s extremely difficult. There’s too much pain and distrust. Old wounds refuse to heal. We can commit it to God our Father, who understands that pain. He enables us to live in His love.

items.title: One Worthy of Worship
items.author: Elisa Morgan
items.summary: One April afternoon, millions gathered along a mapped arc across Mexico and the United States to witness a rare total solar eclipse. Schools released children, small towns blossomed to receive travelers, neighbors set up lawn chairs in driveways donning protective glasses to take in the wonder. As t
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

One April afternoon, millions gathered along a mapped arc across Mexico and the United States to witness a rare total solar eclipse. Schools released children, small towns blossomed to receive travelers, neighbors set up lawn chairs in driveways donning protective glasses to take in the wonder. As television crews documented the countdown to “totality,” the crowd grew silent except for one repeated phrase: “Oh my God!”

That struck me. I don’t know for certain why those observers chose that phrase in that moment, but I suspect that as mortals encountered the rare and the astonishing, they seemed to need Someone to acknowledge. Someone to thank. Someone to worship. When we look heavenward, our response is awe. As David wrote, “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands” (Psalm 19:1).

Luke, the historian, reports Jesus’ last minutes on the cross. “It was about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon, for the sun stopped shining” (23:44-45). Matthew shares a response to this revelation. “When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified, and exclaimed, ‘Surely he was the Son of God!’ ” (Matthew 27:54). They couldn’t help but acknowledge God as the Someone worthy of worship.

In humble awe, I worship You—my God.

items.title: Why Is There a Loneliness Epidemic? Because No One Can Afford to Hang Out Anymore
items.author: Taylor Berry
items.summary: The internet has spent a lot of time trying to figure out why men are lonely. Maybe they don’t have enough friends. Maybe they don’t know how to talk about their feelings. Maybe dating apps broke something. Maybe they need more hobbies. There’s just one problem with the “male loneliness epidemic”: M
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The internet has spent a lot of time trying to figure out why men are lonely. Maybe they don’t have enough friends. Maybe they don’t know how to talk about their feelings. Maybe dating apps broke something. Maybe they need more hobbies.

There’s just one problem with the “male loneliness epidemic”: Men aren’t actually lonelier than women.

Pew Research Center surveyed more than 6,000 American adults and found virtually no gender difference at all. About one in six Americans said they feel lonely or isolated all or most of the time, with roughly equal shares of men and women reporting it.

Harvard’s Making Caring Common project found a similar pattern. Gender wasn’t where the most striking divide showed up — income was.

In Harvard’s nationally representative survey, 29 percent of Americans earning less than $30,000 a year reported loneliness, compared with 19 percent of those earning between $50,000 and $100,000 and 18 percent of those earning more than $100,000. In other words, the loneliness conversation may have been staring at the wrong demographic. Money, it turns out, is deeply connected to who gets to have a social life.

KFF found that 30 percent of adults in households earning less than $40,000 said they “always” or “often” felt lonely, compared with 11 percent of adults in households earning $90,000 or more. Men and women, meanwhile, reported frequent loneliness at similar rates.

The pattern extends beyond the United States. Research across European countries has found the same broad relationship between socioeconomic status and loneliness: The less money people have, the more likely they are to report feeling alone. The important part is what those numbers suggest about the way loneliness is usually discussed. A lot of the conversation treats it as an individual problem. People need better social skills, stronger friendships or more initiative.

But friendships don’t happen in a vacuum. They happen somewhere, and getting there usually costs something.

Even relatively ordinary plans can become expensive quickly. Dinner out. Coffee. A concert. A recreational sports league. Gas across town. A babysitter. None of those expenses is extraordinary on its own. They look different when there isn’t much money left after rent and groceries.

Time can be just as scarce. Harvard found that 62 percent of respondents believed Americans working too much or being too busy or exhausted contributes to loneliness. Its researchers identified younger and lower-income Americans as particularly vulnerable.

There’s an education divide, too. Research from the Survey Center on American Life found that 60 percent of four-year college graduates made a close friend at their alma mater. Among Americans who never attended college, just 35 percent made a close friend through school.

The gap continues at work. More than half of Americans have made a close friend through their workplace or a spouse’s workplace, making the job one of the country’s most important places for forming relationships. But college-educated Americans are more likely to make those friendships: 45 percent have made a close friend through work, compared with 35 percent of people without a college degree.

They’re also more likely to socialize with coworkers outside the office. More than half of workers with postgraduate degrees do so at least a few times a year. Only 38 percent of workers without a college education say the same. That leaves a significant portion of the country with fewer of the places where adult friendships tend to form.

The Survey Center has found college graduates are more likely to develop friendships at work, school, clubs and other membership organizations. Americans without college degrees rely more heavily on their neighborhoods for close relationships. The differences don’t mean the conversation about men and friendship is invented. Pew found real gender differences in how Americans maintain their relationships. Women are more likely than men to turn to friends for emotional support — 54 percent compared with 38 percent — and women with close friends tend to communicate with them more frequently.

Those differences just don’t translate into men reporting more loneliness, but income does.

Pew identifies lower-income Americans among the groups most likely to feel lonely all or most of the time. Harvard found its lowest-income respondents had the highest rates of loneliness. KFF found frequent loneliness was nearly three times as common among adults in households earning less than $40,000 as among those earning $90,000 or more.

None of that establishes a single cause for America’s loneliness problem. It does, however, make the economic divide difficult to dismiss.

items.title: The Dogma of the Assumption
items.author: Dr. Richard DeClue
items.summary:
Dr. Richard DeClue

In honor of the Solemnity of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, here are insights into this beautiful truth and some valuable resources for study.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

On August 15, the Catholic Church celebrates the Solemnity of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary (the “Dormition of the Mother of God” on some Eastern Catholic liturgical calendars). While an exhaustive and conclusive treatment of this dogma—that the soul and uncorrupted body of the Virgin Mary was taken up into heaven at the end of her earthly life—cannot be mounted in a short article such as this, I nevertheless wish, in honor of this solemn feast, to provide some brief insights into this beautiful truth and point the reader to some valuable resources for further study.

Famously, Pope Pius XII defined the assumption of Mary as a dogma on November 1, 1950, in his apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus (Most Bountiful God). Because of the rather recent dating of this dogmatic definition, some people have the false impression that belief in Mary’s assumption is quite novel. In reality, however, Mary’s bodily translation into heaven has been explicitly held by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Oriental Orthodox Christians from very early on. Before the so-called Protestant Reformation, no major ecclesial body denied Mary’s bodily assumption. Actually, even some reformers affirmed Mary’s assumption, such as Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575, a Swiss reformer and the successor of Zwingli).

Although the solemn definition of this dogma occurred via the exercise of papal infallibility, it was anything but a top-down imposition. Quite the contrary, as Pope Pius XII remarks in the document, “When we were elevated to the throne of the supreme pontificate, petitions of this sort [to declare the assumption a dogma] had already been addressed by the thousands from every part of the world and from every class of people, from our beloved sons the Cardinals of the Sacred College, from our venerable brethren, archbishops and bishops, from dioceses and from parishes” (9).

Pius XII had these petitions collected and “carefully evaluated” (10). Their publication took up two volumes (see note 3). Taking this grassroots and universal petition seriously, Pius XII “commanded that, by corporate effort, more advanced inquiries into this matter should be begun” (10). Additionally, he petitioned the bishops throughout the world, requesting their written response to the following questions: “Do you, venerable brethren, in your outstanding wisdom and prudence, judge that the bodily assumption of the Blessed Virgin can be proposed and defined as a dogma of faith? Do you, with your clergy and people, desire it?” (11). They “gave an almost unanimous affirmative response to both these questions” (12).

From a Catholic perspective, that fact alone carries a lot of weight. The teaching of the ordinary and universal magisterium as well as unanimity among all the faithful cannot be in error when asserting that something is to be definitively believed or held (see Lumen Gentium 12 and 25). Hence, in Munificentissimus Deus, Pius XII states: “The concordant teaching of the Church’s ordinary doctrinal authority and the concordant faith of the Christian people which the same doctrinal authority sustains and directs, thus by itself and in an entirely certain and infallible way, manifests this privilege as a truth revealed by God and contained in that divine deposit which Christ has delivered to his Spouse to be guarded faithfully and to be taught infallibly” (12).

The results of intensive studies—both ordered by the pope and conducted by independent academic initiatives—also concluded that the assumption could be dogmatically defined. After all, it was celebrated as a liturgical feast in both the East and West since the patristic era. Many Churches were named after the assumption and/or dormition. It was promoted and taught by Church Fathers and Doctors, saints, and eminent theologians alike. It was already a long-standing mystery contemplated in the Rosary. Without binding the faithful to accept each and every argument offered in favor of the assumption, Pius XII nevertheless cites writings of Church Fathers, statements by popes, and liturgical texts of the undivided Church (i.e., before the schism of 1054).

One of the most well-respected preconciliar scholastic works, the Sacrae Theologiae Summa, cites many of the same and additional sources. With respect to the liturgy, it states: “The feast of the Assumption was celebrated certainly at least from the middle of the 6th century in Alexandria, from the beginning of the 6th century in Jerusalem, from the end of the 7th century in France, from the years 604–687 in Rome, from the 9th century in Spain; more probably also from the close of the 5th century in Jerusalem” (vol. IIIA, 486).

From the existence of such early liturgical development, one can conclude that belief in the assumption goes back even farther. As Pius XII argues: “Since the liturgy of the Church does not engender the Catholic faith, but rather springs from it, in such a way that the practices of the sacred worship proceed from the faith as the fruit comes from the tree, it follows that the holy Fathers and the great Doctors, in the homilies and sermons they gave the people on this feast day, did not draw their teaching from the feast itself as from a primary source, but rather they spoke of this doctrine as something already known and accepted by Christ’s faithful” (20).

Moreover, as Pius XII makes clear, “All these proofs and considerations of the holy Fathers and the theologians are based upon the Sacred Writings as their ultimate foundation” (38). That last statement might be shocking, but it must be kept in mind that traditional biblical interpretation—even with respect to dogmatic questions—does not demand indubitably clear explicit statements about a singular truth. Rather, typology and the entire overarching biblical narrative are valid means of discerning the truth that God is revealing, especially when authoritatively interpreted by the Church. (For more on this, I recommend the book by Dr. Matthew Levering Mary’s Bodily Assumption, especially Ch. 4 on “The Validity and Scope of Typological Exegesis.”)

As one particularly poignant example, Genesis 3:14ff has traditionally been referred to as the protoevangelium (Proto-Gospel), because—from the beginning of the fall—the promise of salvation in Christ is already announced. Notably, this promise pertains not only to the seed of the woman but also to the woman herself. And, as I have written elsewhere, the Church Fathers frequently saw Mary as the new Eve. On this score, the Sacrae Theologiae Summa argues: “In the Proto-Gospel the complete victory of the Redeemer and His Mother are announced. But this victory was not only over sin, but also over death. Therefore Mary had to conquer death completely. But also this complete victory over death is not had except by incorruption and glorious immortality, which is what is meant by the assumption taken formally. Therefore Mary was assumed into heaven” (487). In the lengthier explication of the argument, the authors point to the link between sin and death in Romans 5:12ff as well as in 1 Corinthians 15:21–26 and 15:54–57. The Proto-Gospel is frequently coupled with Revelation 12’s depiction of the savior’s mother, a woman “clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” (12:1), who was taken to a place prepared by God (12:16) saving her from the dragon.

In book five, part two of Matthias Joseph Scheeben’s remarkable Handbook of Catholic Dogmatics, extensive arguments are likewise given, especially in §281: “Mary’s freedom from the dominion or the bonds of death: the singularity of her death, the incorruptibility of her body, and her anticipated resurrection” (579–605). Originally published in German in 1887, this work on soteriology predates the dogmatic definition of the assumption by several decades yet provides incisive arguments in favor of the doctrine’s certitude.

It is additionally noteworthy that Scheeben forms his arguments “primarily according to the biblical-traditional idea about Mary’s dignity and position” (585), which he had already established in an early section of the volume (see §277, 487–501). Among his arguments is the typology seen between “the Ark of the Covenant made out of imperishable wood” and Mary as the new ark (see 591). (See another article of mine on this theme, where the uncanny parallels between 2 Samuel and Luke 1 are shown.) Returning to this motif later in his work, he speaks of “a fully-justified typology when Christians since Modestus and Andrew of Crete have referred the words of Ps 132:8, ‘Arise, O Lord, into thy resting place: Thou and the Ark which Thou has sanctified,’ along with the threefold transfer of the Ark of the Covenant (across the Jordan into the Promised Land, onto Mount Sion, and into Solomon’s Temple), to Mary’s assumption into Heaven, and indeed her bodily assumption, since the Ark of the Covenant is above all precisely the type of Mary’s body” (596). He continues by pointing out the further allusion made in Revelation 11:19: “Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple,” which is the verse directly before Revelation 12:1’s depiction of the woman clothed with the sun, strengthening the connection between the two.

A notable feature of Scheeben’s argumentation is that it goes beyond the idea of mere fittingness. For, as he admits, fittingness shows why something would be sensible but not that it must be the case absolutely speaking (see 593). Much more strongly, Scheeben seeks to show—through his extensive argumentation that goes beyond the scope of this brief article—that the assumption must be true because the corruption of Mary’s body would be wholly unfitting and therefore abhorrent. He writes: “The incorruptibility of Mary’s body is not a question of what is merely fitting (conveniens), whereby the contrary would continue to be conceivable, but rather is a question of what is appropriate (decens), the contrary of which would be perfectly absurd, so that the thought of its possibility makes Christian sentiment shudder” (592). 

His arguments bring together several points already demonstrated throughout earlier sections of his work. In brief, they stem around Mary’s dignity and position with respect to God’s saving plan and her status as the Mother of God. The most succinct summary of his arguments involves what he calls “internal causes of the incorruptibility of Mary’s body” (593), which he divides into four different categories: legal (her freedom from sin), theological (her divine motherhood), economical (an extension of her divine motherhood), and analogical (her perpetual virginity).

While the divine motherhood seems to be the most powerful cause, I will focus here on its economic implications, which strike me as particularly illuminating. Without going into the fully elaborated argument here, I will only quote his succinct statement of the claim: “The economical cause is the same Divine Motherhood, insofar as Mary thereby is the Mother of grace and of all the fruits of grace, therefore also of incorruptibility, and her body is the seat and instrument of the principle of incorruptibility and the means of its union with all mankind” (593). As he writes a little earlier, “The reason which leads to corruption for other human beings comes to nothing in Mary’s case on account of her complete freedom from sin; and if this freedom from sin is also based in turn only on redemption by Christ, then it would nevertheless be quite contrary to the Redeemer’s dignity and the whole economy of redemption if the body which was the seat and instrument of the principle of liberation from all decay, and the means of His union with other redeemed persons, were abandoned to corruption” (591). How could it be that the body from which Christ himself took his flesh and by which he thus united himself to humanity should itself be left to rot in the grave?

In all of these arguments, the assumption of Mary is based upon her relation to her Son, Jesus Christ. It is her unique association with Christ, which no other human has, that leads to her special prerogatives. In this vein, I conclude with the words of Pius XII:

Consequently it seems impossible to think of her, the one who conceived Christ, brought him forth, nursed him with her milk, held him in her arms, and clasped him to her breast, as being apart from him in body, even though not in soul, after this earthly life. Since our Redeemer is the Son of Mary, he could not do otherwise, as the perfect observer of God’s law, than to honor, not only his eternal Father, but also his most beloved Mother. And, since it was within his power to grant her this great honor, to preserve her from the corruption of the tomb, we must believe that he really acted this way. (38)

items.title: Saturday, August 15, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today we celebrate the Solemnity of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Revelation 11:19A; 12:1-6A, 10AB

Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple; and there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
A great portent appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pangs, in the agony of giving birth. Then another portent appeared in heaven: a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and seven diadems on his heads. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and threw them to the earth. Then the dragon stood before the woman who was about to bear a child, so that he might devour her child as soon as it was born. And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. But her child was snatched away and taken to God and to his throne; and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there she can be nourished for one thousand two hundred sixty days.

Psalm
Psalm 45:10, 11, 12, 16

Hear, O daughter, consider and incline your ear;
    forget your people and your father’s house,
   and the king will desire your beauty.
Since he is your lord, bow to him;
    the people of Tyre will seek your favor with gifts,
    the richest of the people
In the place of ancestors you, O king, shall have sons;
    you will make them princes in all the earth.

Second Reading
1 Corinthians 15:20-27

But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died. For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a human being; for as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, after he has destroyed every ruler and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “All things are put in subjection,” it is plain that this does not include the one who put all things in subjection under him.

Gospel Reading
Luke 1:39-56

In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country, where she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me? For as soon as I heard the sound of your greeting, the child in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.”

Reflection

Friends, today we celebrate the Solemnity of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The dogma of the assumption of Mary describes the full salvation of this prime disciple of Jesus.

In the Apostles’ Creed, we speak of our hope for “the resurrection of the body.” Mary, assumed body and soul into heaven, has experienced precisely this resurrection and hence becomes a sign of hope for the rest of the human race.

When we speak of the assumption of the Blessed Mother’s body, we are not envisioning a journey through space, as though Mary moved up into the sky. The “heavens” are a rich and consistent biblical symbol for the transcendent, for a manner of existence that lies beyond our familiar dimensions of space and time.

The assumption of Mary means that the Blessed Mother was “translated,” in the totality of her being, from this dimensional system to the higher one for which we use the term “heaven.” Mary, who exists now in this other world, is not so much somewhere else as somehow else, and this helps to explain why we can speak of her, especially in her heavenly state, interceding for us, helping us, and praying for us.
